sources.title: Country Climate and Development Report: Armenia
sources.temporal_coverage: Country climate and development assessment with observed risk mapping and modeled climate, flood and poverty outcomes through 2060.
sources.methodology: Opened the full 89-page CCDR; it combines spatial risk assessment, flood maps, household data and economic scenarios.
sources.limitations: Mapped losses and projections are model-based; the report notes asset valuation uncertainty for flood-loss estimates.

sources.title: Fourth National Communication on Climate Change under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
sources.organization: Ministry of Environment of the Republic of Armenia, with UNDP support
sources.temporal_coverage: Climate observations and hazard impacts through 2017; crop-yield projections through 2070; adaptation measures mainly reported through 2020.
sources.methodology: Opened the full government communication and reviewed its climate, agriculture and adaptation sections.
sources.limitations: The yield tables do not identify an emissions pathway; reported programs are historical and not independently evaluated.

sources.title: National Action Program of Adaptation to Climate Change and the List of Measures for 2021–2025
sources.organization: Government of the Republic of Armenia, Ministry of Environment
sources.temporal_coverage: Government-approved adaptation action program for 2021–2025, with national and marz-level planning measures.
sources.methodology: Opened the government decree and annex listing adaptation measures, responsible agencies, timelines and indicative financing.
sources.limitations: The program states planned actions, not verified implementation or achieved outcomes; its 2021–2025 period has ended.

sources.title: United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2026–2030
sources.organization: Government of the Republic of Armenia and United Nations Country Team
sources.temporal_coverage: Joint Government–UN strategy for 2026–2030, signed in Yerevan on 19 December 2025.
sources.methodology: Opened the signed framework and reviewed its national rationale and planned green-transition and disaster-risk measures.
sources.limitations: This is a planning framework, not an evaluation; it does not name pilot municipalities or estimate climate-related displacement.

sources.title: Armenia Floods: May 2024 Post-Disaster Needs Assessment
sources.organization: Government of Armenia, United Nations and European Union
sources.temporal_coverage: Multi-sector assessment of the May 25–26, 2024 floods, their impacts and recovery needs in Lori and Tavush.
sources.methodology: Opened the full Government–UN–EU assessment, including human impacts, gender, housing and disaster-risk sections.
sources.limitations: Event assessment; no attribution to anthropogenic climate change or evaluation of long-term recovery.

claims.locator: CCDR, Executive Summary, printed p. 7, and chapter 1, printed pp. 22–24, regional water, land and flood risks
claims.paraphrase: Flood losses relative to regional GDP are highest in Vayots Dzor, Tavush, Lori and Gegharkunik; the report also locates severe irrigation-water and land-degradation risks in high-poverty marzes.
claims.limitations: Flood-loss results are modeled; asset valuation drives some uncertainty.

claims.locator: CCDR, chapter 1, printed p. 20, spatial disparities and fragility risks
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR links spatial disparities with fragility risks, notes high rural and border-region poverty, and says conflict with Azerbaijan raises risks across the economy; it does not identify climate change as causing conflict.
claims.limitations: The report does not establish a climate-to-conflict causal pathway.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The CCDR explicitly associates spatial disparities with fragility risks and states conflict with Azerbaijan raises risks economy-wide; it does not attribute conflict to climate change.

claims.locator: Fourth National Communication, printed pp. 93–94, satellite-based severe-drought damage frequency, 1984–2017
claims.paraphrase: Severe droughts caused at least 30% crop damage in 25% of cases in the Ararat Valley and southwestern Gegharkunik; 50% crop damage was more frequent in Kotayk and Gegharkunik.
claims.limitations: Satellite analysis covers 1984–2017; the reported frequency is not an annual probability.

claims.locator: Fourth National Communication, printed pp. 93–94, Tables 5-7 to 5-9, yield projections by marz
claims.paraphrase: By 2070, projected wheat yields fall about 19–20% in Ararat, Kotayk and Gegharkunik, potato yields 21% in Shirak, while wheat yields rise about 8% in Lori.
claims.scenario: The yield tables describe climate-change projections without agrotechnical measures but do not identify the emissions pathway.
claims.limitations: The cited tables do not state the climate pathway; projections are not local production forecasts.

claims.locator: Fourth National Communication, printed p. 138, pilot crop-insurance program
claims.paraphrase: The communication records a crop-insurance pilot launched in 2018: potatoes and cereals against hail and frost in Shirak, and fruit and grapes in Armavir and Ararat.
claims.limitations: The report records launch and intended coverage, not enrollment, payouts or reduced losses.

claims.locator: National Action Program, printed pp. 10–11, barriers to adaptation
claims.paraphrase: The NAP identifies weak inter-agency coordination and information flows, poor climate integration in public bodies, and gaps in locally relevant risk data and local adaptation finance.
claims.limitations: The NAP describes baseline barriers from consultation, not a later institutional evaluation.

claims.locator: National Action Program, printed pp. 30–32, measures 1.9–1.10 for marz adaptation plans
claims.paraphrase: The 2021–2025 action list scheduled adaptation plans for pilot marzes Shirak and Tavush, then eight more marzes, integrating climate adaptation into regional development planning.
institutions: Ministry of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure
claims.limitations: These were scheduled measures; the NAP does not verify their completion, and its 2025 deadline has passed.

claims.locator: National Action Program, printed p. 19, principle on gender-responsive adaptation
claims.paraphrase: The NAP says social norms can restrict women’s access to climate information, resources and opportunities, and calls for gender-responsive participation in adaptation decisions.
claims.limitations: The principle is generalized and is not a measured marz-specific gender gap.

claims.locator: UNSDCF, printed pp. 23–24, climate risks and potential displacement in the framework rationale
claims.paraphrase: The framework includes possible displacement among the human impacts of climate risks and places climate adaptation within a wider resilience and social-cohesion agenda.
claims.scenario: UNSDCF 2026–2030 planning horizon; no climate scenario or displacement estimate is stated.
claims.limitations: This is a strategic framing, not evidence that climate change caused a specific displacement event.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The framework explicitly identifies potential displacement as a human impact of climate risks.

claims.locator: UNSDCF, printed pp. 45–46, climate adaptation and planned community resilience measures
claims.paraphrase: The UN plans to rehabilitate conflict-affected farmland to reduce resource competition and pilot community-led restoration and efficient water use in border or displacement-affected municipalities to support livelihoods and social cohesion.
claims.limitations: These are planned measures; the framework does not name pilot municipalities or report results.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The framework explicitly links rehabilitation of conflict-affected farmland to reduced resource competition and shared environmental benefits to social cohesion.

claims.locator: May 2024 flood PDNA, printed pp. 35–36, Human Impact and Livelihoods
claims.paraphrase: Lori and Tavush hosted 7% of Nagorno-Karabakh refugees before the May 2024 floods; refugees and host households in Tashir and Alaverdi faced flood-related displacement and damage to homes, food supplies and essential services.
claims.limitations: The PDNA documents flood impacts but does not attribute the event to anthropogenic climate change.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: PDNA names Nagorno-Karabakh refugees among flood-exposed residents in Lori and Tavush and documents impacts alongside host households.

claims.locator: May 2024 flood PDNA, printed p. 38, Gender Insights from affected communities
claims.paraphrase: Field discussions in Lori and Tavush found women-headed households more likely to miss flood compensation when homes or livelihood assets lacked official property registration.
claims.limitations: Focus groups; municipalities lacked disaggregated data on affected residents.

claims.locator: May 2024 flood PDNA, printed pp. 120–122, disaster-risk management impacts and recovery needs
claims.paraphrase: Flooding damaged eight hydrological stations in the Debed and Aghstev basins, impairing water monitoring; the PDNA calls for modern flood forecasting, risk modeling and early warning, especially in remote areas.
claims.limitations: Recommended upgrades are not evidence of completed works.

search_audit.outcome: Opened the CCDR and Fourth National Communication for regional flood, water, drought and crop risks, then reviewed the 2024 flood PDNA for local community impacts.

search_audit.outcome: The CCDR links spatial disparities with fragility risks; the PDNA documents flood impacts among Nagorno-Karabakh refugees and hosts in Lori and Tavush. Neither attributes violence to climate change.

search_audit.outcome: The 2026–2030 Government–UN Framework plans rehabilitation of conflict-affected farmland and shared land and water initiatives to reduce resource competition and support social cohesion; no implementation evaluation was found.

gaps: No existing ARM country baseline was present in the assigned worktree.
The official UNFCCC NDC 3.0 PDF redirect could not be opened; no claims rely on search-index text.

No reviewed primary report establishes that climate change caused conflict or violence in Armenia. The Cooperation Framework states planned resource-competition and social-cohesion pathways, not measured results.
The CCDR's border-conflict context does not identify climate change as a cause of conflict; the May 2024 PDNA records flood impacts but does not attribute the event to anthropogenic climate change.
The NAP's 2021–2025 adaptation measures are plans whose completion was not verified; the Cooperation Framework does not name the border or displacement-affected pilot municipalities.
The Fourth National Communication's crop-yield tables do not identify their emissions pathway; those projections are reported with that limitation.
